It is my hope that this is the case. However, there are still a number of concerns. Here are some that are off the top of my head.

First and foremost is a progressive move to make it harder and harder to remove Secure Boot. For instance, on tablets, as stated, the next version of UEFI explicitly forbids the ability to disable secure boot, which pretty well locks you in in a lot of ways; you may be able to get a few Linux kernels to work, but that's still pretty darn restrictive. This means that Linux-capable hardware will get harder to come by.

This leads to a second point, wherein we end up in a world with highly segregated hardware. This could well end up with a premium price to be paid to be able to boot Linux on your machine, and towards a situation not unlike video game development wherein you had to buy very expensive equipment to run the software on it. This is not an appealing outcome.

A third thing that concerns me is the people who might be able to otherwise explore their computers. Linux investigation often comes from whatever equipment you have, not because you went to purchase a new computer, especially if you are, as I was, young and with no income. This will lead to it being harder to attain technical literacy. While it is somewhat offset by virtualization that is now available (which wasn't available 20 years ago), virtual machines are not a perfect solution by any means.

So it's not quite a death strike I'm anticipating, but more or a progressive corrosion that saps away Linux's potential market and applicability - or that of any non-Windows OS, for that matter.

That depends on your definition of "being forced."

Now it is possible that Windows 7 has some back door that allows a forced update. I have on rare occasion had the system attempt to update itself by surprise, but that was very rare. I heard that it may have had to do something about having an update in the queue at the time the auto-update was turned off.

However, it shouldn't attempt to force it if you turn off updates entirely. And I do mean entirely. I'm not sure what it can do if it downloads them - at the very least it can get you to download a nice big 3 GB chunk of WIndows 10's core without asking you if it auto-downloads.

Now if you mean "forced" as in "in 2020 or so updates stop," that is a factor. However, every copy of Windows 7 in existence will not simultaneously burst into flames then. Rather, new patches won't be made. At that point, there are still options, including using security software and virtual machines. At some point, the chances are high that new software will not support Windows 7, but - with a lot of luck - this will be somehow resolved one way or another by then. For the near future this is not going to be a concern.

As a final disclaimer, I cannot guarantee this, since Microsoft hasn't attempted it. However, for my own Windows 7 machines, I am not particularly concerned.

Any software package of decent size is going to need regular updates as more and more bugs are discovered by users and testers. 99% of updates fix security holes or bugs that would be almost completely invisible to most end users. You only "notice" when something on the front end changes.

I run Malwarebytes, SuperAntiSpyware, and at various times Kaspersky and Bitdefender, both of which I run off CD on a regular basis for full system scans. I have done so for over a decade when using a Windows machine. I set up my anti-virus to be fairly aggressive. When I'm REALLY paranoid I run my browser in a virtual machine. I have yet to find a virus or malware active on this machine, or any other I regularly use, although those security suites have managed to catch more than a few things that would have been nasty. Common sense filled in the rest.

Every last time I've had updates active on Windows, something has gone down in flames horribly. Last time my video card got screwed up so badly I almost had to wipe and reinstall the whole machine. Usually this happens (or happened, not trying it again) within the first two weeks or so of letting updates go of their own accord. On at least one occasion the update process itself knocked the machine offline for around 36 hours processing one single patch.

While I am well aware of the security implications and the multitude of bugs that are patched, I am also aware that Windows is a massive, multi-tentacled monster with pieces of itself flung hither and yon, the output of hundreds of smaller programs produced by many millions of lines of code that comprise it, as well as the numerous ways that access can be re-appropriated. Buffer overflow attacks, fooling the operating system into believing you have administrative permissions, tricking an administrative user into running a program with a bad path environmental variable, sneaking bad parameters into kernel memory to get it to work with bad data that the attacker has provided. Every time you throw a patch into the mix, you risk upsetting the whole thing, and since almost every Windows machine (or any desktop computer) is going to be different, they all have different points where something goes kaboom. Ultimately, I find it a lot better to prevent something from getting close enough to attack it in the first place. As-is, I can only say that I have had and seen many times more problems from updates than viruses. Perhaps I have simply had a unique experience, but I'm very leery about a lot of instant, magical solutions to this sort of thing, and automatic updates sure seem like they fit the bill there. This is especially so since now they carry spyware in the form of Windows 10.
